newsitem.title: UK: Southampton merges to stay with UK soccer big boys.
newsitem.headline: Southampton merges to stay with UK soccer big boys.

text.p: English Premier League soccer club Southampton FC said on Tuesday it was merging with a property company and pushing ahead with plans for a new stadium to guarantee itself a place among the top sides.
Southampton, nicknamed the Saints, has been in the top English division for 18 years but the team is currently third from bottom of the premiership, with 13 points from 17 games.

Its small ground, the Dell, has a capacity of little more than 15,000, with barely any redevelopment space available to cram in more spectators or add revenue-spinning facilities. Vice chairman Keith Wiseman told a news conference the planned new stadium, part of a mult-sport development with retail outlets to the north of the south coast city, was vital to attract good players and revenue.
"It's all about remaining one of the big players in the game," he said.
In the deal announced on Tuesday, the football club is being taken over by Secure Retirement Plc, which started life in 1987 as a builder of sheltered retirement homes.
"Considering the age of some of our players, some fans might say Secure Retirement is an apt company," Nick Illingsworth of the Southampton Independent Supporters' Association said.

But he broadly welcomed the move and hoped it meant money would become available to put new players alongside attacker Matthew Le Tissier, the one real star at a perennially unfashionable and only sporadically successful club.

Wiseman pointed out that manager Graeme Souness, who tasted great success with Liverpool and Glasgow Rangers, had spent some six million pounds ($9.9 million) on six new players this year, and there was no intention of buying a complete new team. Rupert Lowe, the chairman of Secure Retirement, pledged "as much as is needed and can be justified".

Lowe owned up to being a West Ham United fan since his schooldays but said Secure's joint managing director Andrew Cohen had been a Saints fan all his life. "As of now I am a Southampton supporter," he said.

Secure's offer values Southampton at just over 10 million pounds. It will give the football club access to some three million pounds in cash that Secure has available and Lowe was confident further funding could be found.

Wiseman said the timing of the deal was "not entirely coincidental". The regional local authority, Hampshire County Council, is meeting on Thursday and on the agenda is the lease for the 73 acre (29.5 hectares) site of the planned new stadium.
Club officials believed the land deal would be signed if they could show the funding for the development was secured.

The new stadium will cost between 15 and 20 million pounds, but the total development -- including shops, an athletics track, all-purpose football pitches and other sports facilities -- could cost as much as 30 million.

Money from television and from new all-seater grounds has poured into English football in the 1990s and several top clubs are now listed on the stock exchange. Another, Sunderland, announced on Tuesday it would make its market debut on December 24, with a value of 48 million pounds.

Like Southampton, Sunderland is near the bottom of the Premier League but the flotation could provide money for new players and the club is moving to a new 15 million pound, 41,000-seater stadium next season.
